scenario: Your city's largest private employer announced it will close its facility at the end of the fiscal year, removing roughly 9% of general fund revenue. The adopted reserve policy targets two months of operating expenditures; you currently hold about three months. Three councilmembers want to hold service levels flat for two years by drawing reserves down to the policy floor, arguing the economy will recover. Your finance director's forecast shows the gap persisting past year three.
prompt: What is the most defensible course of action for the manager to recommend?

options.text: Recommend the reserve drawdown as requested, since it stays within adopted policy.
options.rationale: Staying within policy is necessary but not sufficient. Using one-time resources to close a structural gap defers the problem and shrinks future flexibility.

options.text: Present a multi-year forecast showing the structural gap, and propose a phased plan pairing limited reserve use with recurring reductions.
options.rationale: Correct. This distinguishes a one-time cushion from a recurring deficit, keeps the council in the decision seat, and makes the tradeoff explicit rather than implicit.

options.text: Refuse to prepare a budget using reserves and require the council to identify cuts first.
options.rationale: The manager advises; the council decides. Refusing to prepare a requested option oversteps the role and damages the working relationship without improving the outcome.

options.text: Propose an immediate across-the-board cut equal to the full revenue loss.
options.rationale: Across-the-board cuts ignore differences in service priority and fixed costs, and moving at full magnitude in year one may be sharper than the situation requires.

explanation: The core distinction is structural versus one-time. Reserves absorb one-time shocks; a permanent revenue loss is structural and must eventually be closed with recurring changes. The manager's job is not to win the argument but to make sure the council decides with the multi-year picture in front of them — which also protects the manager if the forecast proves right.

further_reading.title: GFOA — Fund Balance Guidelines for the General Fund

prompt: In a council-manager form of government, who formally adopts the annual budget?

options.rationale: The manager prepares and proposes the budget but does not adopt it.

options.text: The elected council or governing body
options.rationale: Correct. Adoption is a legislative act.
The finance director builds and administers the budget technically; adoption is not a staff function.
State oversight bodies may review or audit, but do not adopt a local budget.

explanation: The defining split in council-manager government: the council sets policy and adopts the budget; the manager proposes it and then administers it. Getting this boundary right underlies most of the harder judgment questions in this app.

scenario: You are building a five-year capital improvement plan with constrained funding.
prompt: Order these projects from highest to lowest priority using standard asset-management logic.

options.text: Replace a water main with three breaks in the past 18 months
options.rationale: Second. An asset failing repeatedly is already imposing costs — emergency crews, water loss, road cuts — and each break raises the odds of the next one.

options.text: Rehabilitate a bridge rated structurally deficient by the state
options.rationale: First. Life-safety risk outranks everything else on this list, and a deficient rating carries liability and possible load posting that compounds if deferred.

options.text: Resurface a collector street rated fair, before it degrades to poor
options.rationale: Third. This is where the pavement cost curve is steepest: resurfacing a fair street is a fraction of reconstructing a poor one, so deferral multiplies eventual cost.

options.text: Build a new splash pad requested at public comment
options.rationale: Last. A genuine community priority, but adding a new asset while existing ones fail increases the maintenance liability the plan is trying to work down.

explanation: Life-safety risk leads (deficient bridge), then active service failure (repeating main breaks), then preventive maintenance where the cost curve is steepest (fair-condition pavement — deferring it multiplies eventual cost), then new amenities. This ordering is a heuristic, not a rule: strong grant funding or a bundled construction window can legitimately move an item up.

scenario: Assessed valuation in your city is $4.0 billion. The council is considering a rate of $0.55 per $100 of assessed value. Assume a 97% collection rate.
prompt: Estimate annual property tax revenue, in millions of dollars.
explanation: ($4,000,000,000 / 100) x $0.55 = $22,000,000 levied; at 97% collection, roughly $21.34 million realized. The teaching point is the collection rate — budgeting the full levy overstates revenue every year, and the gap compounds. Note also that property tax reacts to market changes on a lag set by your reassessment cycle, so a downturn shows up in the levy one to three years later.

data_reference.source: Illustrative figures — replace with a real municipality's CAFR/ACFR for production use.
data_reference.notes: Good candidates: any city publishing an ACFR with a statistical section showing assessed value and levy history.

scenario: Riverbend's adopted general fund budget is $42.0 million. Finance staff project next year at a $4.6 million shortfall. Two items drive it: the manufacturer's closure removes $3.4 million of recurring payroll, utility, and sales tax revenue, and a settled lawsuit requires a single $1.2 million payment that falls in next year only. Reserves stand at about three months of operating expenditures against a two-month policy floor.
prompt: Split the projected shortfall, then size the reduction the budget must eventually carry.

parts.label: Recurring (structural) share of the shortfall
parts.rationale: The revenue loss is permanent — the payroll, utility, and sales tax base leaves with the plant and does not come back on its own.

parts.label: One-time share of the shortfall
parts.rationale: The settlement is paid once. It is a cash problem next year, not a budget problem every year.

parts.label: Recurring reduction the budget must eventually absorb
parts.rationale: Equal to the structural share, not the headline $4.6M. Sizing the ongoing cut to the full shortfall over-corrects by the one-time item.

explanation: The whole discipline is in the split. Reserves exist to absorb the $1.2M settlement — that is exactly the one-time shock they are for, and using them here does not weaken the position. The $3.4M is different in kind: it recurs, so it has to be closed with recurring changes, and every year it is deferred is a year the reserve is spent buying time rather than absorbing risk. The common error is sizing the ongoing reduction at $4.6M, which cuts services further than the situation requires and is hard to undo politically once done. The tradeoff worth naming: drawing reserves for the settlement is right, and it still leaves less cushion for the next surprise during a period when a rating review is coming.

data_reference.source: Illustrative figures, consistent with the Riverbend case. Replace with a real municipality's ACFR or EMMA official statement for production use.
data_reference.notes: EMMA official statements carry multi-year fund balance history and risk factor sections, which are the right substrate for realistic magnitudes.

scenario: The council passes an ordinance on a subject your city attorney believes is preempted by state law. The state attorney general sends a letter threatening to withhold a state revenue-sharing allocation. Local advocacy groups are publicly urging the council to hold firm.
prompt: As the manager, what do you do in the next 72 hours, and what do you tell staff to do?
explanation: There is no single right answer, and the app should not pretend otherwise. Strong responses typically: (1) get a written legal opinion on the specific exposure and the dollar amount at risk; (2) brief the full council together rather than individually, so no member is surprised; (3) keep the manager's public posture on implementation and cost, not on the policy merits; (4) instruct staff to continue administering existing law until directed otherwise, and document that direction; (5) open a line to state agency staff below the political level. Weak responses commit publicly to a side, or let the council learn the fiscal exposure from the newspaper.
